claim: “With some verbs a manner dependent has the syntactic status of a complement”, as in [4a] She behaved outrageously. In this sense behave requires one, since She behaved on its own is understood as behaving well.
evidence_summary: Ch. 13, p. 1155, agrees: under “(b) Manner complement” it gives [48i] Liz is behaving like a prima donna. But Ch. 4, p. 302 n. 57, on behave among the verbs with an unexpressed reflexive object ([18v]), says that ‘well’ or the like is understood in Behave!, “where no manner adjunct is expressed”.
finding: Medium confidence. The same dependent of behave, with ‘well’ understood when nothing is expressed, is a complement in Chapters 8 and 13 and an adjunct in Ch. 4. The footnote may be loose wording. Or it may follow Ch. 4’s own criteria, since the dependent can be omitted, and then the chapters’ analyses differ. Either way one place needs changing.
inference: Is the manner dependent of behave a complement?

evidence.passage: §2.1, p. 671. “With some verbs a manner dependent has the syntactic status of a complement”.
evidence.establishes: Two chapters call the dependent a complement and a third calls it an adjunct.
evidence.note: Local source (working note, unpublished draft or local copy); not online.
